checks: The apex lies strictly beyond the u-plane for every t>0, and earlier apices lie on the segment from v to later apices. Thus bodies are nested and their u-support strictly increases. A point outside the smaller compact body can be moved a sufficiently small distance toward an interior point of the larger body to get an open ball in the difference. This proves strict volume increase also for d=1.

Using the same convex coefficients and replacing the apex bounds the Hausdorff change by |t−s| times the length of h. Continuity of convex-body volume and the strict increase yield the unique small positive inverse and convergence of its parameter to zero.

For an exterior point, strict separation forces the apex beyond the old supporting plane. The support gap at v is at most t times the length of h, so every limiting normal is u. On subsequences with apex coefficient bounded away from one, the separated inequality forces the old component to approach the singleton u-face. When the coefficient tends to one the point approaches v directly. Compactness upgrades this to uniform locality.

Weak visibility gives the same compactness argument. Distinct marked points have distinct normals because the support face of each normal is a singleton. Finite disjoint normal neighborhoods therefore separate all visible-normal sets simultaneously.

A support face of the multi-apex hull at an exterior boundary point is generated by old support points attaining the new support and apices attaining it. It uses at least one apex and at most one by normal-set disjointness. The ray through any exterior point from an old interior point ends at such a boundary point outside K, proving the union. A common strict separating normal rules out overlaps of the single-apex differences.

readability: The phrase a supporting face uses an apex means that every generating representation of its exterior point uses at least one maximizing apex. The support-value equality makes this immediate.
